newsitem.title: UK: Weather forecasts help cos predict consumer trends.
newsitem.headline: Weather forecasts help cos predict consumer trends.

text.p: British companies are tuning in to weather forecasts, not to find out if employees need to grab an umbrella as they head to work, but to help predict consumer trends in a move that is saving them millions of pounds a year.

"Using detailed weather information, individual stores can save up to 3,000 pounds ($4,890) a week, which means that a supermarket chain can save between 50 and 80 million pounds a year," Viv Ballentine, head of the Weather Initiative, told Reuters on Monday.

Britain's Meterological Office established the Weather Initiative in 1990 as part of its business unit to offer companies the benefit of its long-range forecasting expertise and to develop new sources of funding.

British weather is notoriously unreliable, but using new methodology the Weather Initiative can not only provide long-term weather analysis but can produce complex forecasts of the weather's effect on consumer demand for individual products.

"We are analysing historical sales statistics from research company Taylor Nelson AGB and identifying the weather factors which influenced those sales," said Balalentine. "Mathematical equations are then devised to pinpoint the precise relationship between weather and sales to enable retailers to predict demand much more accurately."
This method allows the Weather Initiative to pinpoint the fluctuations of sales of a single brand such as Unilever's Persil detergent or Nestle's Kit-Kat chocolate bars.
"When the weather changes so do the needs of Britain's stomachs, noses and even pets -- with implications for manufacturers, distributors, retailers and their marketing campaigns," said Ballentine.

If companies know there will be a very hot spell and that sales of mayonnaise or barbecue marinades will increase, they can plan an advertising campaign around that and negotiate media buying rates well in advance, said the Weather Initiative.

The organisation is currently looking at 40 specific product lines including soft drinks, cat food, pork chops, toilet rolls and cold cures. In the next year it will cover up to 1,000 product lines, from air fresheners and deodorants to pickles and vinegar.
Food retailers Somerfield Plc, J. Sainsbury Plc and Marks and Spencer Plc are among the first to sign up for the service.

"If we can't satisfy consumer demand then we lose business," said Jill Rawlings, a spokeswoman for supermarket chain Somerfield "Using the Weather Initiative system we can make sure that products are always in stock when they are needed and that our warehouses are not full of products which consumers don't want."
The system is also helping Somerfield's fresh produce buyers negotiate prices ahead of rivals, she said.
The weather has an enormous effect on consumers' purchasing habits but it is not merely a matter of buying more mineral water in the summer or soup in the winter.

The Weather Initiative's research indicated that canned lemonade sales soar when the thermometer hits 18 degrees Celsius but begin to fall at higher temperatures as consumers seek out cheaper alternatives such as bottles of squash.

The weather also has a big impact on the purchase of toilet rolls and can account for monthly variations in sales of up to 20,000 packs. Sales not only rise in cold weather when millions of people reach for toilet rolls to deal with runny noses but also during hot weather when high pollen counts cause hay fever, Ballentine said.
But it's not just humans who are affected by the weather.

"We have developed a 'cat algorithm' and can predict when they will dive for their (food) bowls," Ballentine said. "When it's wet cats won't go outdoors and they eat more; when it's too hot they won't eat and so food gets thrown away. And when it's really cold they curl up in a ball and forget about food altogether."

Britain's Meterological Office is now looking to expand the system to take account of weather data in other countries to help manufacturers as they become ever more global. It is also investigating how it can help companies in the clothing sector to more accurately predict sales.
